<reason>Both sides were sharp, vivid, and genuinely responsive, and both narrowed the clash rather than widening it. Side A found the best available attack on the motion as written: the "relocation to museums or contextualized sites" clause is the part that makes the policy look like reckoning, and A pressed hard on the realistic outcome (tarp, storage yard, bare plinth), extracting a real concession that a removing-but-not-relocating city has done "half the job." A also offered a genuinely original alternative — additive counter-monuments, renaming, dedication-speech signage — and caught B's scope test shifting between speeches. But Side B did the better job of tracking the proposition's actual decision rule and of weighing. B repeatedly forced the question "should the community keep saying, in its place of honor, that this man deserves reverence?", and A never defended that, which B correctly banked as a structural concession. B then defused the warehouse dystopia cheaply and plausibly (a "contextualized site" can be a fenced lot with panels — a flatbed and printing), and turned the funding objection back on A's newly commissioned, taller bronze. Most decisively, B's closing comparison — "our worst case ends the honor and delays the lesson; their best case delivers the lesson and never ends the honor" — was the cleanest weighing statement in the debate, and it exposed A's admission that the general keeps the plinth "forever" in a reckoning that is "never finished." A's reply that "honor is conferred by framing, not bronze" was the load-bearing claim of its case, and B's flip of it (position is the framing; everything else is caption; you cannot prosecute a man from below) was the single most damaging hit of the exchange. B's Rebuttal 2 being clipped is a real execution cost, but it landed its A1:/A2: answers and its core comparison before the cut. Competitive, but B gave the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's inversion of A's central premise: A claimed "honor is not conferred by bronze; it is conferred by framing," and B answered that twelve feet of bronze on the highest plinth *is* the framing and everything else is caption — "the position acquits him louder than any placard convicts him" — paired with the worst-case/best-case comparison that A's plan, even fully funded, never ends the honor.</best_rebuttal>
